description: We’re Hack Tuah, a team of university students joining the Kuala Lumpur event! We love turning complex ideas into stories people actually care about. Looking for teammates with skills in coding, graphic design, or science/data. Beginners are welcome! Let’s build something fun and meaningful together. 🚀
summary:
Ghost Signals is a scroll-driven web story for readers aged about 9 to 14. Scrolling is travelling: the start page journeys from Earth past the Moon to Mars, and every silent NASA machine is a stop. Opening one starts its chapter, told by the machine itself: Opportunity, built for 90 days and active for 5,111; Ingenuity, planned for five flights and flew 72; Eagle, the Apollo 11 lunar module descent stage left on the Moon; InSight, the lander that listened to Mars for four years; and Sojourner, the first rover on Mars.

Each chapter opens and closes on NASA's own 3D model of the machine, with real NASA photographs between. Every chapter ends with a small game that teaches one true idea, such as dust-storm survival, flying in thin air, timing a laser to the Moon, listening for marsquakes, and planning a drive when commands take minutes to arrive.

It answers the challenge by letting abandoned equipment tell its own story, so children learn why these machines mattered and why they are not forgotten. Every number is checked against a NASA source.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ghost Signals is a scrolling story about five of NASA's silent machines: Opportunity, Ingenuity, Eagle (the Apollo 11 lunar module descent stage), InSight and Sojourner. The start page is a journey outward from Earth past the Moon to Mars, and each machine is a stop. Inside a chapter, the page scrolls through the machine's story. Each chapter opens and closes on NASA's 3D model, with real NASA photographs behind every step in between. NASA has no 3D model of Sojourner, so its chapter uses photographs only.

Every chapter ends with a hands-on game that teaches one real idea:

- Last Light (Opportunity): drive the 3D rover to rocks while a Mars dust storm comes in, and keep it alive.

- Lift off (Ingenuity): spin the rotors in Mars air and in Earth air, to see why Mars's thin air needs much faster blades.

- Find the mirrors (Eagle): fire a laser at the Moon, wait the real 2.5 seconds for the light to return, and find the Apollo sites that left mirrors.

- Listen for marsquakes (InSight): catch faint marsquakes on a drawn seismometer line while wind hides them, then use the dome, then compare with Earth's ground.

- Plan my drive (Sojourner): plan a day's drive on the lander's real photo. Commands took 10 to 15 minutes to reach Mars, so the rover had to drive itself.

HOW IT ADDRESSES THE CHALLENGE

The equipment is the storyteller: each machine tells what happened to it. The narration is labelled as imagined, and what it describes really happened. We show equipment that was left behind and still matters, and we tell its story in a way a ten-year-old can follow.

ACCURACY

Every number and historical claim has a checked entry with a NASA, JPL or NSSDCA source. Where a game number is simplified, the screen says so. There are no invented quotes. Drawn parts are labelled.

WHO IT IS FOR AND WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

Young readers and the adults reading alongside them. Short screens, one true number at a time, large type, and it works on a phone. We hope children finish a chapter knowing one real thing about a machine, and feeling that it was not just abandoned.

ACCESSIBILITY

Keyboard-operable, visible focus, alt text on images, reduced-motion support, readable contrast, and nothing carried by sound alone.

TOOLS

Vite, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, GSAP ScrollTrigger and SplitText (scroll-driven animation), Google's model-viewer (NASA .glb 3D models), three.js (the driving game), sharp, ffmpeg and Pillow (image conversion and alignment), and Claude Code (AI coding assistant).

Source code: https://github.com/rustyjet/ghost-signals
